## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

1	# grow_with_claudinite
2	
3	Opt into the **growth lifecycle** — declaring this pack enrolls a repo in contributing its hard-won
4	lessons up to the shared Claudinite canon, and in pruning its local packs once the canon owns them.
5	Seeded by default (`--init` + the one-time `grow-with-claudinite-seed` baseline migration for the
6	existing fleet), and **opt-out by removal**: baselining never re-adds it.
7	
8	This pack carries the **repo-side** stages of the growth lifecycle: capturing a repo's own
9	lessons into its local packs, and pruning them once the shared canon covers them. The central
10	**promote** stage — which lifts portable lessons up into the shared canon — is a home-only duty
11	that runs canon-side, not a repo-side task, so it lives outside this pack.
12	
13	Its scheduled work is four tasks under this pack's own `tasks/`, each discovered by the repo's
14	scheduler (`engine/scheduler/discover.mjs`) wherever the pack is declared:
15	
16	| Task | Runs when | Where it lands |
17	|---|---|---|
18	| `growth-extract` ([tasks/growth-extract/task.md](tasks/growth-extract/task.md)) | the project changed in the window, or a log is past retention | the repo's own local packs, via a PR that auto-merges after CI, plus the prune on the logs branch |
19	| `growth-dedup` ([tasks/growth-dedup/task.md](tasks/growth-dedup/task.md)) | weekly, when the canon or the project's local packs moved in the week | a PR against the repo's `main` |
20	| `growth-discover-packs` ([tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md](tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md)) | weekly | a new **local** pack in the repo's own `.claudinite/local/packs/`, via a reviewed PR |
21	| `prose-to-checks-sweep` ([tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md](tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md)) | weekly (no-ops cheaply on a quiet corpus) | a PR converting always-testable pack prose into checks |
22	
23	(Plus [usage-fold](tasks/usage-fold/task.md), the agentless daily fold described below.)
24	
25	## Extraction is one task over two sources
26	
27	`growth-extract` is the whole capture stage, and it runs **three skills** in order:
28	
29	1. [extract-from-activity](skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) over the window's commits, merged
30	   PRs and issue discussion;
31	2. [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) over the logs captured
32	   from working sessions (plus the retention prune);
33	3. [prose-to-checks](skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md) over the prose **that run just wrote**, to see
34	   whether any of it upgrades to a check before the PR opens.
35	
36	Everything lands in **one** PR, delivered to land where the repo's delivery settings allow
37	(`engine/scheduler/deliver-pr.md`). The two extraction halves used to be two tasks firing in
38	the same nightly slot against the same local packs; they share the lesson bar, the promotion ladder
39	and the dedup surface ([extracting-lessons.md](extracting-lessons.md)), so the split bought nothing
40	and cost a second opus dispatch, a second PR, and two runs deduping against a corpus the other was
41	concurrently writing.
42	
43	The third step is why the standing `prose-to-checks-sweep` is **weekly**: fresh prose is already
44	offered a conversion the night it is written, so what the sweep sees is a backlog that moves on a
45	weekly clock.
46	
47	A member that wants the local stages without contributing lessons upstream **opts out of
48	promotion** on its own entry — `{ "id": "grow_with_claudinite", "config": { "promote": false } }`
49	— and the central promote stage skips it (absent or `true` = participate).
50	
51	## The conversation lifecycle — capture in-session, extract in the daily task, retention
52	
53	The pack also owns **extraction from working sessions**, replacing the old in-session post-merge
54	lessons pass. Capture and extraction split by what each needs: **capture** needs the live session
55	transcript, so it runs in-session (at merge, and again when the session ends); **extraction** only
56	reads the already-pushed logs, so it is the conversation half of the ordinary `growth-extract`
57	scheduled task — the logs branch is *in the repo*, so reading it, committing lessons to local packs,
58	and pruning are plain local git on the working tree; only posting the summary on the issue uses the
59	GitHub MCP tools.
60	
61	1. **Capture — a step in the merge-to-main skill** (in-session, where the transcript lives).
62	   Right after a merge lands:
63	   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
64	   (in the canon repo itself: `node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`).
65	   Deterministic, seconds; it bundles the session transcript (sidechains inline, timestamp
66	   order), **scrubs enumeration-first** (every value the environment holds — `process.env`
67	   minus a short named allowlist of structural values, plus known credential stores — is
68	   redacted wherever it appears, with credential-shape patterns as the backstop; a secret the
69	   session itself transformed is beyond any static scrub, and push protection is the last
70	   net), and pushes one file per **capture event** onto the orphan **`conversation-logs`**
71	   branch: `<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`, commits marked `[skip ci]`.
72	   **Delta-aware, keyed on the session id:** every capture pushes only the entries after this
73	   session's previous capture, whatever event produced it, so any two events chain into
74	   disjoint files and a zero delta pushes nothing at all. Double-writing is therefore safe by
75	   construction, not by coordination — the property [`session-end.mjs`](session-end.mjs) relies
76	   on, so `pack.test.mjs` pins it directly.
77	   The branch is a **work queue, not an archive** — never merged; tips are cheap in shallow
78	   session clones and retention keeps them bounded.
79	1. **Capture — again, when the session ends** ([session-end.mjs](session-end.mjs), invoked by the
80	   engine's SessionEnd hook runner for every active pack that ships one). Same capture, with
81	   `--issue 0`: **`0` means "no associated issue"**, and the filename shape stays byte-identical
82	   on purpose — the retention prune, the `conversationLogs` signal and the extract's filename
83	   parse all already accept it, whereas a *new* shape would be invisible to the prune and become
84	   immortal on the branch. This event is what captures the sessions that never merge (a review, an
85	   investigation, a session that ended in a question) and the post-merge **tail** of the ones that
86	   do. **Best effort:** a container reclaimed by timeout never fires it, so nothing depends on it
87	   having run — every firing enriches the record, every miss leaves exactly the merge-only
88	   behaviour. An `issue-0` log has no issue for the extract to post its exchange
89	   summary on; nothing else about its lifecycle differs.
90	   **Unattended sessions capture through the same step, deliberately not through the hook.** A
91	   scheduled task's executor session ends by having its container reclaimed, which is exactly
92	   the ending no `SessionEnd` fires on — so the executor runs the engine's runner itself as its
93	   last step and names its dispatch issue in `CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE`, which this step uses in
94	   place of `0`. Those logs therefore file under the task that ran (the dispatch issue's title
95	   names `pack/task`), and the work no human watched becomes as countable as the work one did.
96	2. **Fresh pass — the conversation half of [growth-extract](tasks/growth-extract/task.md)**
97	   (precondition: a substantive merge, or a log actually past retention so the age-based prune still
98	   runs on a quiet repo; local git on the repo's working tree, MCP only for the issue comment). It
99	   applies the [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) skill (the
100	   friction signals and the measured efficiency analysis, computable from the log's timestamps and
101	   token usage) over [extracting-lessons.md](extracting-lessons.md)'s shared bar, routes keepers into
102	   the member's local packs, and posts on the worked issue, for each rule that landed, a
103	   **200-word-max** summary of the slice of conversation that caused it — the dialogue itself is
104	   never pasted there, it is far too verbose for an issue —
105	   **extraction is the only path to permanence**: a log that yields no rule gets no comment,
106	   and its conversation is gone once retention deletes it (a deliberate owner call).
107	3. **Final pass and deletion** — once a log ages past `config.retention_days`, the same task
108	   re-reads it with ~a week of hindsight (the rethink window), then deletes it (the age-based
109	   precondition arm guarantees the prune runs even on a repo gone quiet). Every log gets exactly two
110	   judgment passes. **Unset retention = the prune deletes nothing** (capture-only, fail-safe).
111	
112	No adoption question over it — `retention_days` stays unset (hidden) by default, which is
113	fail-safe (capture-only). A project that wants the prune active sets `config.retention_days`
114	itself (10 is the recommended floor); nothing else to schedule, since extraction rides the
115	fleet's one daily run like the other growth tasks.
116	
117	## Skill-usage metrics — what the mounted skills actually do
118	
119	Mounting a skill only puts its name and one-line description into the session prompt; whether the
120	model ever **loads** it is discretion, and nothing recorded it. So the promotion ladder's
121	skill-vs-prose call had no empirical feedback: a skill whose trigger never fires looked exactly like
122	one that fires daily, and a "skill" that loads in every session (rules wearing a skill's clothes)
123	looked exactly like a genuinely activity-scoped one.
124	
125	The [usage-fold](tasks/usage-fold/task.md) task closes that loop — daily, agentless, seconds. It
126	counts skill loads **and their denominators** (captures, merges, sessions, user messages, user
127	commands) out of the logs this pack already captures, into
128	`.claudinite/local/usage.GENERATED.json`: day rows recomputed statelessly inside the raw retention
129	window, week rows appended once past a `foldedThrough` watermark. Denominators are the point — a raw
130	count cannot tell healthy-rare from broken, so the question is loads *against the sessions where that
131	skill's own declared trigger plausibly applied*. Zeros are implicit (a skill with no loads has no
132	key), which is what makes "never loads" visible: diff the file against the repo's mounted skills.
133	
134	Fleet-wide aggregation is deliberately **not** here — the canon knows mechanisms, never repos. It is
135	the sheepdog pack's [`fleet-usage`](../sheepdog/tasks/fleet-usage/task.md) task, in the fleet-enforcer
136	repo, which is the only place that knows who the members are.
137	
138	## Rules
139	
140	| Rule | Kind | What |
141	|---|---|---|
142	| `growth-config` | hardcoded ([config-check.mjs](config-check.mjs)) | entry config shape valid |
143	
144	**Pack discovery** ([tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md](tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md)) is
145	an ordinary weekly task on the repo's own scheduler. The repo runs the whole pipeline over
146	**itself**: manifest its stack, hold it against the canon packs already on its shelf and its own
147	existing local packs, and — for genuinely project-specific knowledge neither homes — author a new
148	**local** pack populated from its real usage, landed through a **reviewed** PR (a new pack ships new
149	`.mjs` checks, and a check can break CI — the same reason `prose-to-checks-sweep` is reviewed, and
150	the one place this stage differs from extract). It writes only the repo's own
151	`.claudinite/local/packs/`; lifting a local pack up into the shared canon is the central promote
152	task's job.
153	
154	## Identifying a project's capture surface: its local packs (the same way in every stage)
155	
156	Every growth stage operates on a project's **local packs** — the tracked packs a repo keeps under
157	`.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/` (prose in `RULES.md`, checks in the pack's `rules`, activity
158	procedures as the pack's skills, scheduled tasks under its `tasks/`). That subtree **is** the
159	project's own content;
160	the rest of `.claudinite/` is the **read-only mounted canon** and is never a capture, prune, or
161	promote target. So "a project's local packs" means precisely *everything under
162	`.claudinite/local_packs/`, and nothing else under `.claudinite/`*. This is the normalized capture
163	surface — a structural set the stages read the same way, not a `CLAUDE.md`-graph walk over stray
164	Markdown (a repo with no local packs yet simply has nothing to extract, dedup, or promote here; a
165	project adopts the structure via the `generate-project-instructions` skill).
166	
167	Prefer the strongest mechanism the lesson allows — the **local promotion ladder**, applied at the
168	project's own level: a deterministic rule becomes a **check** in the owning pack's `rules` (its
169	failure message carries the lesson), an activity-scoped procedure becomes a **pack skill**, and only
170	what neither can carry lands as **prose** in a pack's `RULES.md`. A check relieves every session's
171	context completely where prose only relocates it, so capture writes *more checks and less prose*.
172	
173	The stages differ only in *how they read that set*, never in *which set it is*: extract and dedup
174	run against the member repo and read the local packs from the working tree; promote runs centrally
175	and reads the same subtree over the GitHub API (get-file-contents under `.claudinite/local_packs/`).
176	Extract writes into it, promote reads from it, dedup prunes within it — all against the identical,
177	`.claudinite/local_packs/`-rooted set.
178

1	---
2	name: extract-from-conversations
3	description: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
4	---
5	
6	# Extract lessons from a conversation
7	
8	The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
9	taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
10	dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
11	what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.
12	
13	The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
14	surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
15	re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.
16	
17	## The goal
18	
19	Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
20	waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
21	cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
22	a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.
23	
24	## Where the conversation comes from
25	
26	- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
27	  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
28	  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
29	  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
30	- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
31	  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.
32	
33	**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
34	when a session is done enough to mine.
35	
36	## What to look for — the friction signals
37	
38	Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
39	necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.
40	
41	### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user
42	
43	The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
44	building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
45	answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.
46	
47	**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
48	user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
49	a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
50	the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
51	correctly **without the round-trip**.
52	
53	### 2. Suboptimal agent actions
54	
55	The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
56	that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
57	something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
58	convention and had it corrected in review.
59	
60	**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
61	so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
62	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
63	first, not after a detour.
64	
65	### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them
66	
67	The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
68	padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
69	hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.
70	
71	**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
72	and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
73	(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
74	only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
75	was already optimal.
76	
77	**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
78	kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
79	the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
80	a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
81	loss of quality.
82	
83	## Encode the questions the user keeps asking
84	
85	The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
86	checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
87	fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
88	fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
89	relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
90	recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
91	retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.
92	
93	## Two passes per log, and the second one may overturn the first
94	
95	A captured log gets a **fresh pass** within a day of capture and a **final hindsight pass** just before
96	retention deletes it, against the corpus as it stands by then. The hindsight pass is a real re-read, not a
97	formality: a friction signal that looked situational the first time may have recurred since, and a lesson
98	landed since may have made a keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes.
99	
100	## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it
101	
102	For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
103	(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
104	nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):
105	
106	- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
107	- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
108	  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.
109	
110	**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
111	beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
112	**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
113	deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
114	silence it replaced.
115

1	# Extracting lessons — the bar and the local promotion ladder
2	
3	> **Scope: what both extraction skills share.** This doc is the **bar** a lesson must clear and the
4	> **ladder** it descends once it clears it — the half that is identical whatever the lesson was mined
5	> from. What each *source* adds is owned by its own skill:
6	> [extract-from-activity](skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) for commits, merged PRs and issue
7	> activity, and [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) for a session's
8	> dialogue. Both load this doc; neither restates it.
9	
10	Its callers are the growth pack's [growth-extract](tasks/growth-extract/task.md) daily task, which runs
11	both skills over one window, and an owner's occasional plain-words ask for a retrospective.
12	
13	## Run the pass on a capable model
14	
15	Extraction is mechanical, but deciding *what clears the bar* is a judgment call a weaker model fails
16	silently — it ships a plausible-but-wrong "lesson" where a capable model correctly bails (see
17	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md), "Match the agent model to the judgment it
18	must make"). The terse rules that *govern* the pass — run it, plus the separate efficiency analysis — also
19	live there; this doc is the how-to.
20	
21	## From signal to lesson — the bar
22	
23	A signal is only worth writing down when the fix is **durable, reusable, and generalizable beyond this one
24	session or window.** Before adding anything:
25	
26	- **Dedupe ruthlessly** against the existing packs — a lesson already covered (even worded differently,
27	  even in another pack, even enforced by a check) is not a new lesson.
28	- **One-offs don't qualify.** A situational detail, a restatement of a generic truism, or something already
29	  implied by an existing rule is below the bar.
30	- **Promote what's portable.** A lesson true for projects beyond this one belongs in shared, cross-project
31	  canon, not stuck in one repo's local packs — the growth lifecycle's promote stage lifts it there
32	  centrally; capture it well locally and let promote generalize whatever travels.
33	
34	## Route to the local pack that owns it — the promotion ladder
35	
36	A project's capture surface is its **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/<pack>/`); everything else
37	under `.claudinite/` is the read-only mounted canon and is never a capture target. Pick the pack whose
38	territory the lesson belongs to (most repos have one general pack; some segregate a domain pack), then
39	prefer the strongest mechanism it allows:
40	
41	1. **A check** in that pack's rules — author the `.mjs`, list it on the pack's `pack.mjs`, ship it with a
42	   red-first fixture. Its failure message *is* the lesson.
43	2. **A pack skill**, when the lesson is an activity-scoped procedure rather than a condition.
44	3. **Terse prose** in the pack's `RULES.md` — only what neither of the above can carry.
45	
46	Write **more checks and less prose**: a check relieves every session's context completely, where prose only
47	relocates it. When no pack's scope fits and the lesson warrants segregation, a new local pack is a
48	self-contained directory drop.
49	
50	**A gotcha tied to one call site is not a pack rule at all.** A trap from misusing a specific API, class, or
51	library goes as a **comment right at the usage site** — next to the call itself, where the next editor of
52	that line sees it — never collected into a centralized gotchas list. Co-locate it in a file's own header
53	comment when the trap spans the whole file and you'd only hit it *while editing that file*. Reserve a
54	central gotchas doc for what no single usage site owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant
55	file (a mistake of omission), or a cross-cutting invariant.
56	
57	## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result
58	
59	Most sessions and most windows yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write
60	nothing rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes the
61	canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a genuinely new,
62	reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.
63

1	# EdFringeNow — project working rules
2	
3	Lessons captured while working in this repo, layered on the shared Claudinite
4	canon. Terse and concrete; read the matching one before working in that area.
5	
6	## The owner asks in plain words — open the issue yourself, before the first commit
7	
8	Work here arrives as a chat request ("Maybe we can just put a 'Show list/Show Map'
9	toggle selector just under the filter…"), never as a filed issue. The
10	`task-lifecycle` check still wants a commit on the branch to reference one, so
11	**open the issue as your first step and put `Closes #N` in the original commit
12	message** — write it from the owner's own words, since it is the only record of
13	what was asked.
14	
15	Leaving it to the stop hook is the expensive path, and it is the path every
16	session took: 7 of the 12 sessions captured on 2026-07-29 declared the work done,
17	got blocked, and then paid create-issue + `git commit --amend` +
18	`git push --force-with-lease` + a second reply that added nothing (#134 33s,
19	#150 45s, #152 35s, #154 43s, #156 43s, #158 57s, #160 20s — ~4.6 min of pure
20	rework). Worse, by then the PR is already open, so the fix rewrites the commit
21	underneath it.
22	
23	## A dispatched run still has to classify its trigger comment
24	
25	The `comment-classification` check reads the last message addressed to you and
26	wants a `Comment class:` line in the reply to it. In a scheduled run that message
27	is the executor prompt ("Execute the Claudinite executor: …"), not anything the
28	owner wrote — but the check does not distinguish them, and it is BLOCKING at the
29	Stop hook. 19 of the sessions captured across 2026-07-29…07-31 were stopped by
30	exactly this finding, every one of them citing the dispatch prompt, and each paid
31	an extra closing reply to clear it (the two runs where the block lands at the end
32	and the cost is cleanly isolable: #183 115s, #160 121s).
33	
34	So **close a dispatched run's final reply with an explicit `Comment class:` line
35	classifying the dispatch itself** — `process-change` for an executor/scheduled-task
36	prompt — instead of discovering the requirement at Stop. On a real owner comment
37	the classification is the substance; on a dispatch it is a formality, but it is
38	far cheaper paid up front than as a second reply.
39	
40	## Read the PR's state, then merge — never loop on `enable_pr_auto_merge`
41	
42	`mcp__github__enable_pr_auto_merge` only accepts a PR whose required checks are
43	still **pending**. This repo's `ci.yml` runs on `pull_request` and finishes in
44	well under a minute, so by the time an agent reaches the arming step the PR is
45	usually already `clean` and the call errors — *"already in clean status (all
46	checks passed) … you can merge directly."* That is not a failure to work around:
47	take it as the answer and call `mcp__github__merge_pull_request` with `SQUASH`.
48	
49	The other refusal, *"in unstable status (required checks are failing)"*, is not a
50	verdict either — a check that is queued, or held at the Actions approval gate,
51	reads identically to one that failed. Re-read the PR
52	(`mcp__github__pull_request_read`) or the run list (`mcp__github__actions_list`)
53	to find out which, and never re-arm on a loop: PR #188 answered "unstable" and
54	then "clean" 27s later with nothing changed in between, and PR #182 answered
55	"unstable" three times across ~4 minutes before answering "clean".
56	
57	The cost is measured. The 2026-08-01 baselining run spent ~350s of its 765s — 4
58	arm attempts, 9 `pull_request_read`s and 5 `ScheduleWakeup` polls — circling PR
59	#182's merge state, and still ended without merging it; the owner merged it by
60	hand the next evening. The same morning's conversation-extract run took its one
61	refusal as an answer and squash-merged 22s later. Check state first, merge
62	directly when it is clean, and arm auto-merge only while checks are genuinely
63	pending.
64	
65	## Verifying UI changes visually (the `index.html` page and everything under `plan/`)
66	
67	Visual verification of the pages **is** available in this sandbox. Don't skip it
68	or downgrade to "verified by logic review only" claiming no browser exists — a
69	browser is here, and a UI change isn't done until it has been looked at.
70	
71	- Serve the repo and drive it with the preinstalled Chromium (or Playwright):
72	  `python3 -m http.server 8000`, then screenshot / click through
73	  `http://localhost:8000`. The app fetches `data/shows.json`, so it must be
74	  served over HTTP rather than opened as a file — and `localhost` bypasses the
75	  agent proxy, so the browser reaches the page even though external hosts need
76	  the proxy.
77	- **Launch Playwright with no `executablePath`, and import from `index.mjs`.**
78	  `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=/opt/pw-browsers` is already exported in this
79	  sandbox, so `chromium.launch()` finds its browser on its own. Every captured
80	  session instead hand-wrote a path and paid for it: `/opt/pw-browsers/chromium`
81	  is a *directory*, and the real binary sits under a version-pinned
82	  `chromium-<build>/chrome-linux/chrome` that moves with the image. Import the
83	  global build by its ESM entry —
84	  `import { chromium } from '/opt/node22/lib/node_modules/playwright/index.mjs'`
85	  (the sibling `index.js` is CJS, so a *named* import from it yields
86	  `undefined`) — or `$(npm root -g)/playwright/index.mjs` if the prefix moved.
87	  Path discovery and its sed-fix-up round-trips cost ~220s across five captured
88	  sessions, every one of them re-deriving the same two facts.
89	- **Keep one browser driver script per session and re-point it.** Authoring a
90	  fresh throwaway Playwright script per screenshot cost 29 heredoc writes and
91	  ~7 minutes of wall clock across the captured sessions (one session alone: 16
92	  writes, 4.5 min). Write the driver once into the scratchpad, take the URL,
93	  selector and output path from `process.argv`, and re-run it — a re-run is
94	  seconds where a rewrite is 15–20s.
95	- To build a `/plan` favourites list for the render, a plain slug-per-line text
96	  file is accepted by the parser — pick shows spanning the statuses (and some
97	  same-day doubles) you want to eyeball.
98	- **Known-noisy console output from the served page.** A page driven off
99	  `python3 -m http.server` reliably logs a `favicon.ico` 404 (the repo ships
100	  none) and often `net::ERR_CONNECTION_RESET` as the browser tears down. Neither
101	  is an application error — filter both out of a smoke script's error assertion
102	  so that a red run means something, rather than sending you chasing a phantom
103	  404 through extra browser runs.
104	- To match edfringe.com's live styling (e.g. the ticket-availability colours on
105	  the `/plan` grid), fetch the official site's CSS with `curl` through the agent
106	  proxy and read the palette out of it. `WebFetch` returns rendered text without
107	  the CSS, and headless Chromium cannot tunnel the proxy to reach an external
108	  host — `curl` is the one path that works for off-box assets.
109	
110	## The live site is reachable — check real state at `*.edfringenow.com`, allowing for CDN lag
111	
112	The environment's egress policy allows `*.edfringenow.com`, the live site's own
113	domain. So a question about what the deployed site actually serves — is the new
114	field in `data/shows.json`? did the deploy land? — is answerable directly, with
115	`curl https://www.edfringenow.com/…` through the agent proxy, rather than by
116	reasoning from the working tree. General egress is still closed: everything
117	*except* the allowed domain fails the same way, so this is a single-domain
118	window, not open internet.
119	
120	Two caveats before you trust what comes back:
121	
122	- **The response is CDN-cached, so a fresh push may not be visible yet.** A
123	  200 with stale content is not evidence the deploy failed — re-check after a
124	  delay, and never conclude "the change didn't ship" from one read taken
125	  seconds after the push.
126	- **Confirm the allowance is live in *your* session before relying on it.** The
127	  policy is per-environment and a session can be running under an older one; on
128	  2026-08-07 a probe of both `www.edfringenow.com` and the apex returned
129	  `curl: (56) CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403`. A 403 at CONNECT is a policy
130	  denial, not a site outage — `curl -sS "$HTTPS_PROXY/__agentproxy/status"`
131	  lists the recent rejections and confirms which it is. When it's denied, say so
132	  and fall back to the repo, rather than reporting the live site as down.
133	
134	As with the off-box CSS fetch above, `curl` is the working path: headless
135	Chromium cannot tunnel the proxy, and `WebFetch` returns rendered text rather
136	than the raw JSON or asset you usually want here.
137	
138	## The site is two front-ends — cross-page behaviour goes in `shared/`
139	
140	The Now page (`index.html` + `js/app.js`) and the planner (`plan/` + `plan/plan.js`)
141	are separate front-ends, and `plan/lib/` is the planner's own engine, not a common
142	library. But both are now ES modules, so **anything that must behave the same on
143	both pages belongs in `shared/`** and is imported by each — never copy-pasted.
144	Both pages spell the import the same way (`../shared/geo.js` resolves to
145	`/shared/geo.js` from either), so moving a value there is a small change.
146	
147	What is still genuinely twinned (untangled the same way when next touched): the
148	header `debug v<version>` pill, the Now/Plan nav, and the haversine in
149	`plan/lib/travel.js` that was ported from `js/app.js`.
150	
151	A shared module needs **no** `package.json` to mark it as ESM: the pinned Node 22
152	detects module syntax in a `.js` file by itself, with no warning and no flag, so
153	`node --check` and the test suite both handle it. `plan/package.json` predates
154	that detection and its stated reason (silencing a module-detection warning) no
155	longer applies; it is harmless, so it stays, but do not copy it as a pattern —
156	the `edfringe-no-stray-package-json` check flags any other one.
157	`.js` and `.mjs` are both served as `text/javascript` by `python3 -m http.server`,
158	so the extension is a style choice — use `.js`, matching `plan/lib/`.
159	
160	A new top-level source dir must be added to `scripts/verify.sh`'s `git ls-files`
161	list, or nothing in it is ever parse-checked — the `edfringe-verify-sh-covers-source-dirs`
162	check catches an omission. Note that `git ls-files` only sees *tracked* files, so
163	a new file silently sits outside the syntax sweep until it is committed — the
164	"checked N files" count is not evidence your new file was among them.
165	
166	## `.claudinite/shared/` is generated output — never hand-resolve its conflicts, always take the fresher version
167	
168	## A pack rule or check encodes a *work procedure*, never product behaviour
169	
170	Rules and checks in `.claudinite/local/packs/` are about **how work is done here**
171	— the gate that must stay wired, the tool that must be launched a certain way, the
172	files that must move together. **Product behaviour is not a rule.** What the site
173	does — which ticket statuses count as unavailable, what the Now page shows, how
174	far "walkable" reaches — is a **requirement**, and it belongs in the requirements
175	spec (`product/requirements.md`, the `executable-requirements` pack) and its
176	tests, never in a pack's `rules`.
177	
178	The trap is that product behaviour reads exactly like a good check candidate: it
179	is deterministic, statically detectable, and genuinely worth enforcing, so a
180	prose-to-checks sweep will happily convert it. The 2026-07-30 sweep did: it turned
181	the `ticketStatus`-not-`soldOut` rule into an `edfringe-ticket-status-unavailable`
182	check, with a clean scoped parse and a see-it-fail proof against mutated real repo
183	content — a well-built check of the wrong kind, which the owner rejected on sight
184	("Rules shouldn't be about product requirements, only work procedures"). The
185	sibling conversion in the same PR, `edfringe-normalizer-selftest-in-verify` ("the
186	offline self-test must stay wired into `verify.sh`"), was the right kind and
187	stayed.
188	
189	Apply the test **before** writing the check, since the build quality of the check
190	tells you nothing about whether it belongs: *if the product changed its mind
191	tomorrow, would this rule be wrong?* If yes it is a requirement — a red check
192	would then be reporting a product decision as a process violation, and the
193	requirements spec is where that decision is already supposed to live. If instead
194	it would still hold because it describes how we work regardless of what the
195	product does, it is a rule. Prose in a `RULES.md` gets the same test: the
196	`ticketStatus` paragraph in the `edfringe-data` pack is background a scraper
197	editor needs, not a rule, and it is not convertible.
198

1	# EdFringeNow — the data pipeline (scraper/ and data/)
2	
3	The domain of this pack: getting show data out of edfringe.com and into the
4	committed files the site serves. Read it before touching `scraper/` or anything
5	under `data/`. The API's own field reference lives in
6	[scraper/SCRAPING.md](../../../../scraper/SCRAPING.md) and the file layout in
7	[scraper/README.md](../../../../scraper/README.md) — this is the working
8	judgment those two don't carry.
9	
10	## The live API is unreachable from a session — don't try, and don't fake it
11	
12	`edfringe-tikketr-web-api.equhost.com` is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy and
13	`edfringe.com` returns 403 to `WebFetch`. So: no session — this one included —
14	can verify a scraper change against live data. Anything that must touch the API
15	runs through a sanctioned workflow: the `Scrape edfringe shows (full)` workflow
16	(`.github/workflows/scrape.yml`), `Fetch ticket prices (one-off)`
17	(`prices.yml`), or the `refresh-shows` / `refresh-tickets` scheduled tasks.
18	Never "verify" a scraper change by reasoning about what the API probably
19	returns — either have a sanctioned workflow run it, or say plainly that it is
20	unverified.
21	
22	The egress block is a **policy boundary, not an obstacle to route around**. Do
23	not create ad-hoc GitHub Actions workflows — push-triggered "probes" or
24	anything else — to reach the API (or any blocked host) from an open-network
25	runner: that is CI as a side channel around the session's network rules. For
26	one-off API questions (a field's shape, an enum's value set, a sample payload),
27	`scraper/SCRAPING.md` is the reference; if the answer isn't there, ask the repo
28	owner rather than building a bypass.
29	
30	`python3 scraper/normalize.py --selftest` is the one transform check that runs
31	offline; it exercises raw→master→day-file→`shows.min.json` on a fixture, so a
32	normalizer change is verifiable here even though a fetch change is not. Because
33	it is the only offline verification a scraper change can get, it must stay wired
34	into `scripts/verify.sh` — the `edfringe-normalizer-selftest-in-verify` check
35	enforces that (a step *label* naming the self-test does not count; only a command
36	line does).
37	
38	## `ticketStatus`, never the `soldOut` boolean
39	
40	"Can I get a ticket" comes from the per-performance `ticketStatus`, not the
41	`soldOut` flag: a performance can be `soldOut: false` and still have nothing to
42	sell online (`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE`). The site treats `SOLD_OUT` and
43	`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` as unavailable and everything else as available
44	(`NO_TICKETS_STATUSES` in `js/app.js`), and unknown means available. Any new
45	availability logic — client or scraper — keys off `ticketStatus`; `soldOut` is
46	carried through for display only.
47	
48	## Prices are fetched once, and "unknown" is a third state the encoding must keep
49	
50	`data/prices.json` is a fetch-once cache (`scraper/fetch_prices.py`), off the
51	nightly path: a show's price bands are set when it goes on sale, unlike its
52	ticket status. `refresh-shows` reads the cache and carries the amounts through
53	untouched — it never re-fetches them. So the festival keeps adding shows the
54	cache has never seen, and **a show with no price is a normal, permanent state of
55	the data**, not a gap the pipeline should close.
56	
57	Which means the encoding carries three states, not two, and every stage has to
58	preserve the distinction:
59	
60	| state | master | wire |
61	|---|---|---|
62	| costs nothing | `priceMin: 0` | `pm: 0` |
63	| priced | `priceMin: 22.5` | `pm: 22.5` |
64	| unknown | `priceMin: null` | no `pm` key at all |
65	
66	`priceMin: 0` and `free: true` are **not** the same claim and don't always agree.
67	The flag comes from the listing; the £0 can also come from the price API, which
68	returns a single `Price band 1` at £0.00 for a handful of shows the listing
69	doesn't flag free — pay-what-you-want, or a box office that never set a price
70	(10 of 3,664 in the first full run). Both readings are honest about what a ticket
71	costs, so the price path keys off `priceMin`, and `free` stays what the *listing*
72	said. Don't "fix" one to match the other.
73	
74	Never encode unknown as `0`, and never let a decoder default it to one: a stage
75	that collapses three states into two is lying about money, and nothing
76	downstream can recover the difference. What the site then *does* with an unknown
77	price is a product decision, not a pipeline one — it lives in `shared/price.js`.
78	
79	Two traps in the raw price payload, both already handled and both worth not
80	re-introducing: amounts arrive as **strings**, and nearly every show carries a
81	£0.00 "Personal Assistant" concession (a carer's companion ticket) that must not
82	be read as the cheapest price. See the pricing section of
83	[scraper/SCRAPING.md](../../../../scraper/SCRAPING.md).
84	
85	## The committed data is generated output — regenerate it, never hand-edit it
86	
87	`data/raw_pages/` is a git-ignored regenerable cache. `data/normalized/`,
88	`data/venues.json` and `data/days/` **are** committed, because the browser
89	fetches them — but they are still generator output. Fix the data by fixing
90	`scraper/normalize.py` and re-running it (`--merge` for a top-up, no flag for a
91	full rebuild from the raw cache); a hand-edit is silently overwritten by the next
92	`refresh-shows` run and leaves the bug in the generator.
93	
94	`data/prices.json` is the one exception, and it is an exception to the *direction*
95	rather than the rule: it is committed, but it is normalize.py's **input**, written
96	by `scraper/fetch_prices.py`. Nothing regenerates it on a schedule, so nothing
97	overwrites a hand-edit either — which is precisely why editing it by hand is still
98	wrong: the edit survives, silently disagreeing with the box office forever. Re-run
99	the fetch. The `edfringe-data-dir-is-generator-output` check allows it **by name**,
100	so a second file can't ride in on its shape.
101	
102	## Changing the wire format is a four-file change
103	
104	The day files and `shows.min.json` reference `data/venues.json`'s global lists
105	**by position** (`genre`, `room`, `subs`, `ts`; `g`, `rm`, `sg`, `ar`). That
106	encoding has one producer and two decoders, and they must move together:
107	
108	- producer — `scraper/normalize.py` (`build_lookups` / `build_day_files` /
109	  `minify_master` / `build_availability`)
110	- decoder 1 — `js/app.js` `adaptShow`, for the day files
111	- decoder 2 — `plan/lib/hydrate.js` `rehydrateShows`, the exact inverse of
112	  `minify_master`, round-tripped against the real committed files by
113	  `plan/lib/__tests__/hydrate.test.mjs`
114	
115	Add or drop an indexed field and all three change in the same commit. That the
116	indices still *resolve* is enforced by the `edfringe-lookup-indices` check — it
117	catches a lookup list regenerated without its day files, but nothing can catch a
118	decoder left reading the old key, so check both decoders by hand.
119	
120	Two properties of that encoding are load-bearing for caching, and both fail
121	silently:
122	
123	- **The lookup lists are append-only** (`extend_lookup`). The browser holds
124	  `shows.min.json` for four days and `venues.json` for one, so a stale catalogue
125	  is routinely decoded against a newer lookup file. An entry that changed index
126	  would relabel shows' genres and rooms with no error anywhere. Entries are never
127	  dropped, even once the master stops using them.
128	- **`shows.min.json` carries nothing that changes through the day.** Ticket
129	  status lives in `availability.min.json` (its own status list, indexing into
130	  nothing, so the hourly refresh can rewrite it alone). Putting a status back in
131	  the catalogue would restart its hourly churn *and* freeze availability for
132	  anyone holding a cached copy — the bug in #249, re-created from the other end.
133	  `hydrate.test.mjs` asserts each wire performance carries only `d` and `s`.
134	
135	The same three-way move applies to plain (non-indexed) wire keys such as the
136	price fields `pm` / `px`, with one extra hazard: the round-trip test compares the
137	rehydrated record to the master **as JSON**, so a new master key has to appear in
138	the *same position* in `normalize_event`'s dict and in `rehydrateShows`'s object
139	literal. Adding it in one place and appending it in the other fails the
140	round-trip on key order alone, which reads as a data bug and isn't one.
141

These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](../packs/) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

One or the other always gets the box: the done-signal when nothing remains, the open-items list when something does.

=== worker.sh ===
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# refresh-tickets worker — the ported body of the retired "Refresh today's ticket
# status (hourly)" workflow's job.
#
# The Claudinite scheduler runs this as its `prework` subprocess with
# cwd = this task directory and a hard kill at `prework_timeout`, so
# the first thing it does is move to the repo root the scheduler hands it. There
# is no agent: a non-zero exit is the failure signal, and the scheduler converges
# that to one open `needs-human` issue (the old job's `report-failure` twin).
#
# It only reaches here when task.mjs's precondition says the Edinburgh clock is in
# August, between 08:00 and 23:59 — that gate is the whole of the retired
# workflow's sixteen cron lines. The script itself stays a no-op on any date with
# no day file, so a mis-timed run costs nothing.
#
# Python: the scheduler workflow is a vendored thin shim and cannot carry a
# `setup-python` step, so this uses the runner's own `python3` rather than the
# retired workflow's pinned 3.11. The scraper is standard-library only, so any
# maintained 3.x satisfies it; the guard below fails loudly if there is none.
set -euo pipefail

cd "${CLAUDINITE_REPO_ROOT:-$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)}"

if ! command -v python3 >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "refresh-tickets: no python3 on the runner" >&2
  exit 1
fi

# Return the checkout to `main` before touching anything. The scheduler runs
# EVERY due task in ONE checkout, and `basics/baselining`'s deliver() does
# `git checkout -B <maintenance branch>` and never switches back — so a task
# ordered after a delivering baselining inherits a branch that has no upstream,
# which is what killed the push with exit 128 in #231 and #141 (both slots where
# baselining delivered first). Switching back here — BEFORE the scraper writes
# anything — puts the commit on the branch it was always meant to land on.
# Not `git push origin HEAD:main`: from a polluted checkout that would push
# baselining's unreviewed converge straight to main, past its maintenance PR.
current_branch="$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD)"
if [ "$current_branch" != "main" ]; then
  echo "refresh-tickets: checkout was left on '$current_branch' — returning to main." >&2
  git checkout main
fi

# The retired workflow exposed a `date` dispatch input for testing; a task has no
# inputs, so the scheduled default (today onward, Europe/London) is the only mode.
# A one-off is still available by hand:
# `python3 scraper/refresh_ticket_status.py --date 2026-08-10`.
python3 scraper/refresh_ticket_status.py

git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
git config user.email "github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
# `data/normalized` is what makes this reach the planner at all: the script now
# writes fresh statuses through the master and regenerates from it, so the file
# the planner actually loads (availability.min.json) is in this commit. Staging
# only the day files — as this did until #249 — meant the hourly refresh
# succeeded every hour and changed nothing the planner could see.
#
# The bulky catalogue is staged too but will not normally appear in the diff:
# it carries no ticket status any more, so regenerating it over an unchanged
# master reproduces it byte-for-byte. That is deliberate — a catalogue that
# stopped churning hourly is what lets the browser cache it for days.
git add data/normalized data/days data/venues.json
if git diff --staged --quiet; then
  echo "No ticket-status changes this hour."
else
  # Not "today's" any more: the refresh covers today through the end of the run
  # (#249), so the old subject would have understated every commit it made.
  git commit -m "Refresh ticket status"
  # `main` is the branch actions/checkout created and set tracking on, so a bare
  # push resolves correctly; the guard above is what guarantees we are on it.
  git push
fi

90	  fresh throwaway Playwright script per screenshot cost 29 heredoc writes and

- **Launch Playwright with no `executablePath`, and import from `index.mjs`.**
  `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=/opt/pw-browsers` is already exported in this
  sandbox, so `chromium.launch()` finds its browser on its own. Import the
  global build by its ESM entry —
  `import { chromium } from '/opt/node22/lib/node_modules/playwright/index.mjs'`
  (the sibling `index.js` is CJS, so a *named* import from it yields
  `undefined`) — or `$(npm root -g)/playwright/index.mjs` if the prefix moved.
  Path discovery and its sed-fix-up round-trips cost ~220s across five captured
  sessions, every one of them re-deriving the same two facts.
  `/opt/pw-browsers/chromium` is a **symlink** onto the version-pinned
  `chromium-<build>/chrome-linux/chrome`, so it is a valid `executablePath` if
  you ever need one — but you don't, and the pinned build under it moves with
  the image.
- **Never `npm i playwright` into the scratchpad to make the import resolve.**
  A bare `import { chromium } from 'playwright'` in a scratchpad script fails
  with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` — the global install is not on the resolution
  path, and `NODE_PATH` does not apply to ESM, so exporting it changes nothing.
  The obvious next move is the wrong one: a fresh `npm i playwright` pulls a
  **newer** Playwright than the image's, which then hunts for a browser build
  the image does not ship (`chromium_headless_shell-1234` against the vendored
  `-1194`) and dies asking for `npx playwright install` — a download the
  sandbox cannot make. Three sessions on 2026-08-07 (#251, #258, #264) each
  took that detour and then backed out of it. Use the absolute path to the
  global build: it is the one matched to the vendored browsers.

1	# Delivering a scheduled task's pull request
2	
3	How an executor subagent delivers the PR its task produced — the AGENT lane of the one
4	delivery procedure. The CODE lane is `land-pr.mjs` beside this file (Action-side workers
5	run it); **the two must keep saying the same thing** — a nuance changed in one changes in
6	the other in the same commit. Your GitHub writes go through the session's MCP tools, and
7	your pushes ride a credential whose events start workflows normally, so — unlike the code
8	lane — your PR's checks need no help from you to run.
9	
10	## The task sets the ceiling; the repo decides the rest
11	
12	Your task's declared `expected_outcome` is a **ceiling, not a plan**:
13	
14	- **`open-pr`** — open the PR and stop. Never arm auto-merge, never merge. Nothing below
15	  applies to you.
16	- **`merged-pr`** — the task *may* land its PR. Whether it actually lands unreviewed is
17	  **this repo's** setting, read in step 1 — never the task's own knowledge. The same task
18	  lands itself on one repo and waits for an owner on another, and both are correct.
19	
20	## 1. Read the repo's delivery preference
21	
22	`.claudinite-checks.json` → `maintenance.delivery`:
23	
24	- **`auto-merge`** (legacy aliases `auto`, `push`) — go to step 2.
25	- **`review`** (legacy alias `pr`) — leave the PR open for the owner and stop. Never arm
26	  it, never merge it, and never read the standing PR as a failure: degrading `merged-pr`
27	  to open-pr is the repo's stated intent, and member config wins.
28	- **Missing or empty** — proceed as `auto-merge` (the default). Do **not** write the key:
29	  materializing it is baselining's converge job, not yours.
30	- **Anything else** — someone stated an intent you cannot honour, and guessing could
31	  deliver its opposite. Leave the PR open (the posture that merges nothing) and name the
32	  unrecognized value in your wrap-up comment on the dispatch issue.
33	
34	## 2. Arm auto-merge
35	
36	Arm GitHub's native auto-merge on the PR — **squash**, always. Armed → done: GitHub lands
37	it once this repo's required checks pass.
38	
39	## 3. When the arm is rejected
40	
41	- **"Pull request is in clean status"** — the base branch requires nothing, so auto-merge
42	  has no queue to wait behind and this arm will be rejected every time. That is a repo
43	  *shape*, not an error — nothing needs fixing, and the merge is yours to make: once any
44	  checks that did start on the PR's head have **concluded green**, merge it yourself
45	  (squash). A repo with no PR checks at all merges as soon as the PR is mergeable.
46	- **Any other rejection** ("auto-merge is not allowed", "unstable status", …) — judge on
47	  evidence, exactly as the code lane's landing pass does. Read the workflow runs on the
48	  PR's **head sha**:
49	  - A run parked at `action_required` **never ran** — it is neither a pass nor a failure;
50	    ignore it and judge by the runs that actually executed.
51	  - Wait (within your run's time budget) for the real runs to conclude. Everything
52	    concluded, nothing failed, at least one succeeded → merge (squash).
53	  - Anything genuinely failed (`failure`, `timed_out`, `cancelled`, `startup_failure`),
54	    or the runs won't conclude inside your budget, or GitHub refuses the merge itself
55	    (a required gate you could not see) → **leave the PR open** and say why in your
56	    wrap-up comment, naming the repo settings a human should check: Settings → General →
57	    "Allow auto-merge", and Settings → Actions → General workflow-approval requirements
58	    (the usual source of the parked `action_required` run). A PR left open with its
59	    reason stated is a *delivered* outcome within the `merged-pr` ceiling — the trail
60	    survives and the task's next cycle (or the owner) picks it up; a merge past a red or
61	    unseen check does not survive anything.
62	
63	## Never
64	
65	Merge with anything but squash; merge while a real check is failing or still running;
66	arm or merge when the repo said `review`; write `maintenance.delivery` yourself; or
67	manufacture a merge to satisfy the ceiling — "no change" and "left open, reason stated"
68	are always legal outcomes.
